standards.all: All lists every serializer measured for the languages you picked, public formats and private ones together. The value exists so the whole field is visible in one place when you are choosing a library. Choosing a named standard narrows that list to codecs that speak one format.
standards.custom: No public spec means the library invents its own bytes. These codecs were written so one language, or one program, could save objects quickly without agreeing on a format other people publish. Typical uses are caches, session state, and local files. Another language usually cannot read the payload.
standards.json: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for objects, arrays, numbers, strings, and booleans. It grew out of JavaScript object literals in the early 2000s so browsers and servers could exchange data without a schema file. Typical uses are web APIs, configuration, and logs. It is easy to read and widely supported. Binary formats are usually smaller.
standards.yaml: YAML is a text format meant to be easier for people to edit than JSON or XML. It was created for configuration, with indentation, comments, and less punctuation. Typical uses are application settings, CI pipelines, and Kubernetes manifests. Many documents can also be read as JSON. The extra syntax makes parsers slower and less alike.
standards.toml: TOML is a text configuration format with named tables and simple assignments. It was created so config files stayed obvious, without YAML's indentation rules. Typical uses are tool settings and package manifests, such as Cargo.toml and pyproject.toml.
standards.cbor: CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a binary form of the JSON data model. It was standardized so small devices and network protocols could send JSON-like values in fewer bytes. Typical uses are IoT, security tokens, and embedded protocols. A reader needs a CBOR library. It does not need a separate schema file.
standards.msgpack: MessagePack is a binary encoding of the same kind of values as JSON: maps, arrays, strings, and numbers. It was created to make JSON smaller and faster on the wire. Typical uses are RPC between services, caches, and logging. Field names usually travel with the data, so a reader can ignore a field it does not know.
standards.protobuf: Protocol Buffers is a schema-first binary format from Google. It was created so services could add fields over time without breaking old readers. You write a .proto file and generate code for each language. Typical uses are gRPC APIs and long-lived service data. The bytes are compact. A reader needs the field numbers from that schema.
standards.avro: Apache Avro is a binary format that keeps the schema with the data, often in a file header or a schema registry. It was created for pipelines that store years of records and still need to add fields. Typical uses are Kafka topics, Hadoop files, and event logs. A reader uses the writer's schema to decode older data.
standards.bson: BSON (Binary JSON) is the document format used by MongoDB. It was created so a database could store JSON-like documents with lengths and extra types, including dates and raw bytes, that are quick to scan. Typical uses are MongoDB documents and their drivers. Outside that ecosystem it is less common than JSON or MessagePack.
standards.flatbuffers: FlatBuffers is a binary format a program can read in place, without unpacking the bytes into new objects. It was created for games and other software that must touch data with very little overhead. Typical uses are game assets, telemetry, and large tables passed between processes. A schema defines the layout. The reader walks offsets inside the original buffer.
standards.ion: Amazon Ion is one data model with a text form and a binary form. It was created at Amazon so systems could keep rich types, such as timestamps, decimals, blobs, and annotations, and still move documents between languages. Typical uses are service payloads and storage inside Amazon systems. A reader can skip fields it does not know.
standards.ubjson: UBJSON (Universal Binary JSON) is a binary encoding of the JSON data model with explicit sizes on values. It was created as a simple binary JSON so a parser could allocate once and skip values it does not need. Typical uses are embedded and application data where a text JSON document is bulky and a separate schema is unnecessary.
standards.smile: Smile is a binary JSON format from the Jackson project. It was created so Java services that already spoke JSON could send the same values in fewer bytes without a different data model. Typical uses are Jackson-based HTTP and messaging. After the first message, repeated field names can be shortened.
standards.kiln: Kiln is a schema-first binary format for records and numeric blocks, including a read that borrows an array from the encoded buffer. It exists so machine-learning and array workloads can share one wire contract across languages. Typical uses are tensors, a block of model weights, and a request that carries both metadata and arrays.
standards.thrift: Apache Thrift is a schema and RPC system first built at Facebook. It was created so many languages could call the same service from one interface definition. Typical uses are internal RPC. This benchmark times the serialization layer. A reader needs the generated schema.
standards.capnp: Cap'n Proto is a schema-based binary format whose in-memory layout matches the bytes on the wire. It was created to remove the pack and unpack step that Protocol Buffers and Thrift perform. Typical uses are low-latency RPC and messages passed between processes. A reader follows pointers inside the original buffer.
standards.bond: Microsoft Bond is a schema-based serialization system for services. It was created so services could evolve data contracts across languages, with schemas that can also be read at runtime. Typical uses are service payloads and logs. Bond has compact and fast binary layouts, and a JSON encoding of the same schema.
standards.bebop: Bebop is a schema-based binary format aimed at small messages. It was created as a compact contract with code generation and little work on the hot path. Typical uses are multiplayer game messages and typed client/server payloads.
standards.hocon: HOCON (Human-Optimized Config Object Notation) is a JSON superset for configuration. It was created for the Typesafe stack so config files could include comments, substitutions, and includes. Typical uses are application configuration on the JVM, especially Play and Akka. It is a text format for people, not a compact wire format.
standards.plist: Property List is Apple's structured data format, in XML and in a binary form. It was created for preferences and bundles on Apple platforms. Typical uses are app settings, Info.plist metadata, and local persistence. Outside Apple systems JSON is the more common choice.
standards.zon: ZON (Zig Object Notation) is Zig's text format for data and configuration. It exists so Zig programs can store structured values with the standard library, in syntax that matches the language. Typical uses are Zig build data and config. It is a language format, not a cross-language standard.
standards.arrow: Arrow IPC is the columnar format from Apache Arrow, written as a stream or a file. It was created so data systems could share columns of numbers and strings without converting each row into a new object. Typical uses are handing tables between query engines, data frames, and Arrow Flight. A reader that speaks Arrow can use the column buffers directly.
standards.parquet: Apache Parquet is a columnar file format. It was created so analytics jobs could read only the columns they need from very large tables, and compress similar values together. Typical uses are data lakes, Spark, and warehouse exports. It is a file of many rows, not a codec for one web request.
standards.orc: Apache ORC is a columnar file format from the Hive ecosystem. It was created for the same scan-heavy analytics job as Parquet, with its own stripes, indexes, and types. Typical uses are Hive and other warehouse tables. Like Parquet, it targets files of many rows.
standards.sbe: Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) is a schema-based binary layout from the FIX trading community. It was created so trading messages could be encoded with fixed offsets and almost no copying. Typical uses are market data and order messages. The schema fixes where each field sits. It fits records whose shape is stable.
standards.hdf5: HDF5 is a file format and library for large scientific arrays. It was created so researchers could store multidimensional numbers, with groups, attributes, and partial reads, in one portable file. Typical uses are simulations, instruments, and machine-learning datasets. This suite times an array, not the five small records.
standards.netcdf: NetCDF is a file format for array-oriented scientific data, often stored on top of HDF5. It was created so climate, ocean, and atmosphere data could be shared with named dimensions and coordinates. Typical uses are gridded measurements and model output. A reader can ask for a window of the grid instead of the whole array.
standards.adios2: ADIOS (Adaptable IO System) is a library for large simulations to write arrays efficiently, including in parallel. It was created so supercomputer jobs could move huge timesteps to storage. Typical uses are HPC simulations and later analysis of those outputs. This benchmark times the array path.

data_sets.suite: The suite is the publication set: five small record shapes, measured at one record and at one hundred. It exists so every language can be compared on the same everyday payloads: a flat message, a nested document, numeric telemetry, a block of strings, and an event envelope. Typical uses of these shapes are APIs, documents, metrics, and logs. This is the default data set.
data_sets.columnar: The columnar set is wide tables and one aligned trading-style record. It exists because a five-field message does not show the difference between a row serializer and a column file. Typical uses are scans over many rows, reading one column out of a wide table, nested rows, and market-data messages. Only libraries that can carry these shapes are measured here.
data_sets.graph: The graph set is one object network with shared nodes and a cycle. It exists because most codecs store trees, and a tree cannot represent two fields that point at the same object. Typical uses are object graphs inside one process, such as a document whose records share a child. Libraries that only write trees are absent from this set.
data_sets.array: The array set is one dense grid of numbers, plus a read of a window inside that grid. It exists so scientific file formats are compared on the job they were built for, instead of on a small message. Typical uses are images, maps, and simulation grids. The five suite records are not part of this set.
data_sets.tensor: The tensor set is machine-learning payloads: a float matrix, a borrowed read of that matrix, a token prompt, a block of weights, and a request that wraps them. It exists because document codecs and tensor codecs are built for different shapes. Typical uses are model serving, training checkpoints, and inference requests. A borrowed read uses the encoded bytes in place.

data_types.message: A message is one flat record of mixed fields: booleans, integers, floats, and short strings, with no nested objects. It is in the suite as the cheapest structured payload, so the cost of the library itself is visible. Typical uses are a status update, a user record, or a simple API body.
data_types.document: A document is a nested record: an id, a status, a small map, and a list of line items. It is in the suite because many real payloads are trees, and nesting costs more than a flat struct. Typical uses are an order, a stored document, or an API response with a list inside.
data_types.telemetry: Telemetry is one reading made mostly of numbers: a source, a timestamp, a few tags, and a list of values. It is in the suite to show numeric bulk rather than nested structure. Typical uses are a sensor sample, a metric point, or a monitoring row.
data_types.strings: The strings type is a list of text and almost nothing else. It is in the suite to show the cost of encoding and copying text, without a complicated record around it. Typical uses are a batch of names, log lines, or search tokens.
data_types.event: An event is a small envelope: an id, a type, a time, a producer, and a few attributes. It is in the suite as the shape of a log line or a message-bus record. Typical uses are an audit event, a click, or a trace span. One hundred events in one call is a batch.
data_types.table: A table row is a wide flat record: sixteen floats, four integers, and two strings. It exists so columnar files and row codecs can be timed on a scan-shaped row, not on a tiny message. Typical uses are a feature row, a measurement row, or a warehouse record.
data_types.table_project: Table project writes the same wide row as table, and the read returns only the first float column. It exists because columnar formats are built to skip the columns a query does not need, and a full-row read hides that. Typical uses are a query that needs one measure from a wide table.
data_types.nested_table: A nested table is one struct plus a list of structs. It exists because column formats shred that nesting into columns, which a flat row does not exercise. Typical uses are an order with line items, or an event with a repeated group, stored as a table.
data_types.signal: A signal is a fixed header, then short strings, then a repeating group. It exists as the aligned record Simple Binary Encoding was designed to pack, and as a check that other codecs can carry the same shape. Typical uses are a market-data tick or an order update.
data_types.graph: A graph is shared region nodes plus a ring of people who point at one another. It exists because a tree encoding cannot store one object reached by two fields, or a cycle. Typical uses are an object network in memory, such as orders that share a region. Libraries that only write trees do not appear on this type.
data_types.grid: A grid is one 512 by 512 array of 64-bit floats, written and read in full. It exists so array file formats are timed on a real grid rather than on a handful of fields. Typical uses are a raster, a map layer, or a simulation field.
data_types.grid_window: Grid window writes the same array as grid, and the read returns only an interior rectangle. It exists because scientific formats can fetch a window without copying the whole array. Typical uses are viewing a region of a map or a tile of a larger field.
data_types.tensor: A tensor is one 1024 by 1024 matrix of 32-bit floats, including a negative zero and a quiet NaN, read back as an owned copy. It exists as the plain path that returns the matrix. Typical uses are an activation, an embedding table, or a batch of features.
data_types.tensor_view: Tensor view is the same matrix as tensor, and the read borrows the payload from the encoded buffer instead of copying it. It exists to show designs that avoid a second allocation. Typical uses are serving a weight or an activation without copying the matrix.
data_types.prompt: A prompt is padded token inputs: token ids, an attention mask, and position ids, as integer matrices. It exists because model servers send tokens, not one float matrix. Typical uses are a batch of prompts waiting for inference.
data_types.shard: A shard is one transformer block of 32-bit weights: an embedding, attention, a feed-forward layer, and a norm. It exists so a checkpoint-shaped payload is in the set, not only a single matrix. Typical uses are saving or shipping one layer of a model.
data_types.request: A request pairs a request id, a model name, and a temperature with the prompt tensors. It exists because a real inference call is metadata plus tensors. Typical uses are an inference request body.

views.batch: Batch size is {n}. One call writes and reads that whole batch. Size 1 is a single message or request. A larger size is a page of logs or telemetry sent together.
views.batch_compound: This row averages the {nA}-record call and the {nB}-record call for this same data type. A library can be quick on one record and slower on a batch. Both results stay in the score.
views.all_n: This row averages the five suite records at {n} per call: message, document, telemetry, strings, and event. It is one score for everyday payloads. Tables, graphs, arrays, and tensors stay in their own data sets.
views.all_all: This row averages every suite record at every batch size. It is the broadest single score for the publication set. Tables, graphs, arrays, and tensors stay in their own data sets.
